results.title: Importance Sampling and Variance Reduction Techniques | by Diogo Ribeiro | Data Science as a Better Idea | Medium
results.content: Importance sampling is a method used in Monte Carlo simulations to reduce the variance of estimates of certain quantities, thereby increasing their accuracy [1]. The importance distribution g(x) should be chosen such that it is similar to the function f(x) p(x), as it will reduce the variance of the estimate. For instance, in rare-event simulation, where we want to estimate the probability of an event that occurs very rarely under the original distribution p(x), importance sampling can be particularly useful [3]. Besides importance sampling, several other techniques aim to reduce the variance of Monte Carlo estimators, including antithetic variates, control variates, stratified sampling, and bootstrapping. While there are many methods available, you might be wondering how the variance reduction techniques such as importance sampling can be used for outlier detection. Variance reduction techniques like importance sampling, antithetic variates, control variates, stratified sampling, bootstrapping, and more advanced techniques like quasi-Monte Carlo methods, multilevel Monte Carlo methods, and the CFTP method, have made significant contributions to the field of statistics and computer science.

# Using control variates & antithetic method with Monte Carlo. Supposing $g(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$, I want to calculate the expected value of g, $E(\sqrt[3]{x})$, using Monte Carlo method, by generating $x\_i$ from a Weibull distribution with parameters $(1,5)$. After that, I want to use the **control variates method** and the **antithetic method** in order to to reduce the variance of my estimator, which I found with the simple Monte Carlo. Using Matlab, I found the expected value $S$ by generating 1000 random numbers from the `weibull(1,5)` distribution and calculate the sum. $\begingroup$ @jbowman the part i was given is only the simple monte carlo, but i read that it's not the best method to estimate the expected value. There is no one way to implement either control or antithetic variates, however, a couple of examples may help. Antithetic variables: Imagine instead of the random number generator you actually used, you generated a $U(0,1)$ variate, call it $u$, and ran it through the inverse CDF of the Weibull(1,5) distribution, thereby generating a Weibull(1,5) variate. This helps to "balance" high and low values from your random number stream, thus reducing variability of your final estimates. Control variates: These are "extra" variables that are correlated with the result, enabling you to do something like run a regression on your results against the control variates to get a more accurate estimate. In your case, for example, you know the true mean of the Weibull dist'n (5), so you could use the $x\_i$ as a control variate. answered Dec 10, 2011 at 15:43. $$ Therefore, you can implement the antithetic method by using a sample of uniforms, $U\_1,\ldots,U\_n$ and its complent $1-U\_1,\ldots,1-U\_n$ and compare the variance of the estimator of $\mathbb{E}[X^{1/3}]$ with the corresponding estimator based on $U\_1,\ldots,U\_{2n}$. The control variate is implemented in your case by choosing a known moment of the Weibull, for instance as suggested by jbowman, $$ \mathbb{E}[X] = \lambda \Gamma(1+1/k) $$ and using $X$ as the control variate. Again, checking the improvement brought by the control variate requires a Monte Carlo experiment with several runs. answered Dec 11, 2011 at 10:08. results.title: Variance Reduction Techniques of Importance Sampling Monte Carlo Methods for Pricing Options
results.content: Variance Reduction Techniques of Importance Sampling Monte Carlo Methods for Pricing Options\*. **Keywords:** Monte Carlo Method; Importance Sampling; Variance Reduction; Option Pricing. In this paper we discuss the importance sampling Monte Carlo methods for pricing options. Motivated by this thought, several techniques to reduce the variance of the Monte Carlo simulation have been proposed, such as control variates, antithetic variables, importance sampling and stratification(see Boyle, Broadie and Glasserman [1], and Glasserman [2]. An early example of importance sampling applied to security pricing is Reider [7], where the variance was reduced substantially by increasing the drift in simulation for deep out-of-the-money European call options. Numerical results in table 1 show estimated prices and variance ratios, relative to ordinary Monte Carlo method, using importance sampling with GHS method and the new method respectively, which confirm the effectiveness of the procedure for this problem, especially for in-the-money options. In this paper, a new importance sampling Monte Carlo method for pricing options is proposed.
